questions.question: Which law states that equal volumes of all gases contain the same number of molecules when under the same conditions of pressure and temperature?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Avogadro's Law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Avogadro's Law** states that under identical conditions of temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases contain an equal number of molecules.
 
• The law mathematically relates the volume (V) of a gas to the number of molecules (n), expressed as V ∝ n (at constant temperature and pressure).
 
• This principle is crucial in understanding molecular behavior and has been foundational in deriving the ideal gas law.
 
• **Avogadro's number**, 6.022 × 10²³ molecules per mole, is derived using this law and is a fundamental constant in chemistry.
 
• The law applies universally to all ideal gases, irrespective of their chemical composition, making it a pivotal concept in gas laws and stoichiometry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Terminologies:**

 
 
• **Avogadro's number:** Represents the number of molecules in one mole of a substance, approximately 6.022 × 10²³.
 
• **Mole concept:** A standard unit in chemistry to express the amount of a substance, crucial for stoichiometric calculations.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Avogadro's Law:**
 
 
• Used to calculate molar volume of gases, which is approximately 22.4 liters for one mole of gas at standard temperature and pressure (STP).
 
• Helps in determining molecular weights of gases by comparing their densities under similar conditions.
 
• Forms the basis of the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, which integrates Avogadro's law with other fundamental gas laws.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Proposed by Amedeo Avogadro in 1811 to explain the behavior of gases and their molecular compositions.
 
• Initially met with skepticism, Avogadro's hypothesis gained acceptance only after Stanislao Cannizzaro's work in 1860.
 
 
 
• **Limitations:**
 
 
• Avogadro's law strictly applies to ideal gases; real gases deviate from this behavior under high pressure and low temperature.
 
• Intermolecular forces and finite molecular sizes in real gases cause deviations from the ideal gas assumptions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Charles's Law **states that at constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.
 
• **Boyle's Law **describes the inverse relationship between pressure and volume at a constant temperature, meaning as pressure increases, volume decreases.
 
• **Faraday's Law**, from electromagnetism, states that a changing magnetic field will induce a voltage (or electromotive force) in a coil of wire.

questions.question: Which mountain range is the youngest in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Himalayan Range** is the youngest mountain range in India and the world, formed approximately 50 million years ago during the Cenozoic Era.
 
• It was created due to the collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate, resulting in a tectonic uplift.
 
• The Himalayan Range is still tectonically active, with ongoing movement of the Indian Plate causing earthquakes and geological changes. *Hence, option 3 is correct.*
 
• **The Himalayas** include several peaks, such as Mount Everest, Kanchenjunga, and Nanda Devi, making them a prominent geographical feature of India and South Asia.
 
• The range spans across northern India and extends into Nepal, Bhutan, and Tibet, serving as a natural barrier and influencing the region's climate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Eastern Ghats**

 
 
• Description: A discontinuous series of hills broken by rivers flowing into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• Location: Along the eastern coast of India, passing through Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu.
 
• Highest Peak: Arma Konda (or Jindhagada Peak) in Andhra Pradesh.
 
• Biodiversity: Rich in flora, but generally less so than the Western Ghats. 
 
 
 
• **Western Ghats**
 
 
• Description: A continuous, more continuous, and geologically older mountain range that acts as a major watershed.
 
• Location: Along the western coast of India, stretching from Gujarat to Kerala.
 
• Highest Peak: Anamudi in Kerala.
 
• Biodiversity: Known for very high biodiversity, with dense evergreen forests and being the origin for major rivers like the Godavari and Krishna. 
 
 
 
• **Satpura Range**
 
 
• Description: An east-west running range composed of the Satpura, Mahadeo, and Maikala hills.
 
• Location: In central India, across states like Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat.
 
• Highest Peak: Dhupgarh.
 
• Significance: Considered a structural uplift or "horst" and has a significant forest cover that provides habitat for endangered species.

questions.question: As per the (April-June) 2020 data released by the National Statistical Office (NSO), India's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for the April-June quarter (Q1) slipped by what percentage?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India's GDP for Q1 (April-June) 2020 fell by 23.9%:** This was the steepest quarterly contraction since the country began reporting GDP data, primarily due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
 
• The decline was driven by a massive drop in economic activity across sectors like manufacturing, construction, and trade during the nationwide lockdown.
 
• **Construction and manufacturing sectors:** These sectors saw a contraction of 50% and 39%, respectively, contributing significantly to the GDP fall.
 
• The services sector, which accounts for nearly 60% of the GDP, also showed a sharp contraction, with trade, hotels, transport, and communication shrinking by 47%.
 
• **Agriculture sector:** The only bright spot was the agricultural sector, which grew by 3.4% during the same period, benefiting from favorable monsoon conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP):**

 
 
• GDP refers to the total monetary value of all goods and services produced within a country's borders over a specific time period.
 
• It is a critical indicator used by policymakers to assess the economic health of a nation and plan fiscal and monetary policies.
 
 
 
• **Impact of COVID-19 on India's Economy:**
 
 
• The nationwide lockdown imposed to curb the spread of the virus severely disrupted economic activity, leading to job losses and reduced consumer spending.
 
• Several sectors, including tourism, hospitality, and retail, faced prolonged shutdowns, impacting their contribution to GDP.
 
• The demand for essential goods and services remained relatively stable, but non-essential sectors suffered significant contractions.
 
 
 
• **Recovery Measures:**
 
 
• The government introduced fiscal stimulus packages, including credit schemes and direct benefit transfers, to revive economic activity.
 
• The Reserve Bank of India implemented monetary policy measures like reducing the repo rate and providing liquidity to financial institutions.
 
• Gradual reopening of economic activities in the latter half of 2020 helped mitigate the impact of the contraction.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with other economies:**

 
 
• India's GDP contraction of 23.9% was one of the sharpest globally during Q1 2020, highlighting the severity of the pandemic's impact.
 
• Other major economies like the US and UK also reported significant GDP contractions, though India's was more pronounced.
 
 
 
• **Long-term implications:**
 
 
• The contraction highlighted the need for structural reforms to improve resilience in critical sectors like manufacturing and services.
 
• It also emphasized the importance of diversifying the economy and promoting digital transformation to mitigate future shocks.
 
• The agricultural sector's positive performance underscored its role as a stabilizing factor during economic crises.

questions.question: Who among the following laid the foundation of the Kushan Empire in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2) Kujula Kadphises**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kujula Kadphises** was the founder of the Kushan Empire in India during the 1st century CE.
 
• He united the fragmented Yuezhi tribes under a single rule and established a strong empire in Bactria, which later expanded into northwest India.
 
• Kujula Kadphises laid the foundation for the Kushan Empire's dominance in Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Under his reign, the Kushan Empire became a significant power, facilitating trade routes, especially along the Silk Road.
 
• His conquests laid the groundwork for the cultural and economic prosperity that flourished under his successors, like Kanishka.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vima Kadphises**

 
 
• Succeeded Kujula Kadphises and expanded the empire east of the Indus, into the Mathura region.
 
• He was a follower of Shaivism, as shown by his coins.
 
• Minted gold coins and used titles such as "Lord of the Whole World".
 
 
 
• **Kanishka**
 
 
• The most powerful and famous Kushan ruler, who reigned from approximately 78 to 101/102 CE.
 
• Extended his rule from Central Asia to North India and conquered Kashmir.
 
• Supporter of Buddhism, patronised scholars like Vasumitra, Asvaghosa, and Nagarjuna.
 
• His reign is associated with the Shaka era.
 
 
 
• **Huvishka**
 
 
• Kanishka's successor, who kept the empire intact.
 
• Was a patron of both Buddhism and Zoroastrianism.
 
• Credited with building many Buddhist monasteries and stupas.
 
 
 
• **Vasudeva I**
 
 
• The last significant ruler, whose reign saw the decline of the empire in some regions.
 
• A worshipper of Shiva.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India is associated with 'Promotion of international peace and security'?

__
 
• **Article 51** of the Indian Constitution comes under the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV).
 
• It directs the state to work towards **promoting international peace and security**.
 
• The article emphasises maintaining **just and honourable relations** between nations.
 
• It further advocates for respect towards **international law and treaty obligations** in dealings with other countries.
 
• Lastly, Article 51 encourages the promotion of **settlement of international disputes by arbitration.**

• Added four new DPSPs: Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (participation of workers in industry management), Article 48A (protection of environment and wildlife), and Article 39(f) (opportunities for healthy development of children).
 
 
 
• **44th Amendment Act, 1978:**
 
 
• Added a new clause (2) to Article 38, stating the state shall strive to reduce inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities.
 
 
 
• **86th Amendment Act, 2002: **

__
 
• **Progressive Achievement of Self-Reliance** was a primary goal of the **Fourth Five-Year Plan** in India, implemented between **1969 and 1974**.
 
• This plan emphasized achieving **economic stability** and reducing dependence on foreign aid by boosting domestic production and enhancing self-sufficiency.
 
• The plan aimed to achieve a growth rate of 5.7%, focusing on **agriculture, industrial development, and export promotion**.
 
• **The Green Revolution** was an integral part of the Fourth Plan, which significantly increased agricultural productivity, particularly in wheat and rice production.
 
• The plan also aimed to tackle problems of **poverty and unemployment** by promoting rural development and small-scale industries. *Hence, option 3 is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969–1974):**

 
 
• This plan was prepared during the tenure of **Indira Gandhi**, and it was influenced by the need for self-reliance following India's wars with China (1962) and Pakistan (1965).
 
• It sought to address the challenges of **economic instability** caused by inflation and the aftermath of droughts in the 1960s.
 
• The plan allocated significant resources to agriculture, with a focus on irrigation, fertilizers, and high-yield variety seeds under the Green Revolution.
 
 
 
• **Key Achievements:**
 
 
• The Green Revolution led to a sharp increase in food grain production, making India self-sufficient in food grains by the early 1970s.
 
• The plan emphasized the development of **basic industries** such as steel, petroleum, and chemical fertilizers to reduce reliance on imports.
 
• It also promoted rural development programs such as integrated rural development to enhance the living standards of the rural population.

__
 
• **The Barind plains** are primarily located in **West Bengal, India**, specifically in the northern part of the state, near the districts of Malda, Murshidabad, and Dinajpur.
 
• This region is part of the **eastern Indo-Gangetic plains**, characterized by its slightly elevated and older alluvial deposits.
 
• The Barind plains are known for their **low fertility** due to the presence of older alluvium and high clay content, which reduces water retention.

questions.question: In the cell cycle, which of the following stages is NOT a part of Interphase?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 3 (Mitosis)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Interphase** is the phase of the cell cycle in which the cell prepares for division and is divided into three stages: **Gap 1 (G1), Synthesis (S), and Gap 2 (G2).**
 
• The **Mitosis phase** is separate and distinct from Interphase. It involves the actual division of the cell into two daughter cells.
 
• During Interphase, the cell grows, DNA replicates, and organelles are duplicated, making it ready for mitotic division. *Hence, Mitosis is NOT part of Interphase.*
 
• Interphase is considered a preparatory stage, while Mitosis is an active division phase. *Thus, Option 3 is correct.*
 
• The Interphase stages (G1, S, G2) focus on growth, replication, and preparation for division, whereas Mitosis focuses on the segregation of genetic material.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Stages of Interphase:**

 
 
• **Gap 1 (G1):** The cell grows and synthesizes proteins and organelles necessary for DNA replication.
 
• **Synthesis (S):** DNA replication occurs, doubling the genetic material to prepare for cell division.
 
• **Gap 2 (G2):** The cell continues to grow and prepares for Mitosis by producing proteins needed for chromosome segregation.
 
 
 
• **Mitosis:**
 
 
• Mitosis consists of four stages: **Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, and Telophase.** These stages lead to the division of the nucleus and its genetic material.
 
• It is followed by **Cytokinesis,** where the cytoplasm divides, forming two daughter cells.
 
 
 
• **Cell Cycle Overview:**
 
 
• The cell cycle is divided into two main phases: **Interphase** (G1, S, G2) and **M phase** (Mitosis and Cytokinesis).
 
• Interphase constitutes the majority of the cell cycle, with M phase being relatively shorter.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Interphase:**
 
 
• Interphase ensures the cell is adequately prepared for division by growing, replicating DNA, and synthesizing necessary proteins.
 
• It is critical to prevent errors in DNA replication or cell division, which can lead to mutations or cell death.

The correct answer is __**4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 213** of the Indian Constitution grants the Governor the **power to promulgate ordinances** when the state legislature is not in session.
 
• The Governor can issue ordinances only if they are necessary to take immediate action under the circumstances.
 
• Ordinances issued by the Governor are considered temporary laws and must be presented before the state legislature **within six weeks of its reassembly**.
 
• These ordinances cease to operate if they are not approved by the legislature within the stipulated time or if they are withdrawn earlier.
 
• The Governor cannot promulgate an ordinance that contains provisions that would require the assent of the President without obtaining prior permission.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **What is an Ordinance?**

 
 
• An ordinance is a law promulgated by the executive (Governor or President) when the legislature is not in session, enabling the executive to address urgent matters.
 
• It is intended to function as a temporary measure and must be approved by the legislature within a specified time to continue as law.
 
 
 
• **Governor’s Legislative Powers:**
 
 
• Apart from issuing ordinances, the Governor summons and prorogues the sessions of the state legislature and can dissolve the state legislative assembly.
 
• The Governor can also reserve certain bills for the consideration of the President.
 
 
 
• **Limitations on Ordinance-making Power:**
 
 
• The Governor cannot promulgate an ordinance on matters that fall outside the purview of the state legislature.
 
• An ordinance cannot contravene the provisions of the Constitution and must align with legislative competence.

questions.question: What does the 11th fundamental duty, which was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, deal with?

options.text: Providing opportunities for the education of children
Preservation of the rich heritage of the country
Protecting and improving the natural environment
Upholding and protecting the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The 11th Fundamental Duty was** added by the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002**, which made it a duty of every citizen to provide opportunities for education to their child or ward aged 6-14 years.
 
• ** This specific duty ensures that parents and guardians play an active role in ensuring that children in the age group 6-14 years are provided with education.
 
• This amendment aligns with the Right to Education Act, 2009**, which ensures free and compulsory education for children in this age group.
 
• The 11th Fundamental Duty emphasises the role of citizens in supporting the nation’s goal of achieving universal education as a fundamental right under Article 21A of the Constitution.
 
• This duty is aimed at strengthening the education system and encouraging citizens to actively contribute to the intellectual development of children.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fundamental Duties:**

 
 
• Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• Initially, there were 10 Fundamental Duties, but the 11th was added through the **86th Amendment Act, 2002**.
 
• These duties are outlined in **Article 51A** and serve as moral obligations for citizens to contribute towards the nation’s development and uphold constitutional values.
 
 
 
• **Right to Education Act, 2009:**
 
 
• Also known as the **RTE Act**, it ensures free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years as a fundamental right under **Article 21A**.
 
• The act mandates 25% reservation for disadvantaged children in private schools and ensures infrastructure and teacher standards to promote quality education.
 
 
 
• **86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002:**
 
 
• This amendment introduced **Article 21A**, making education for children aged 6-14 years a fundamental right.
 
• It also added the 11th Fundamental Duty under **Article 51A(k)**, compelling citizens to provide educational opportunities to their children.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Relation between Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles:**

 
 
• While Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, they complement the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which aim to establish social and economic democracy.
 
• The duty to provide education aligns with the DPSP under **Article 45**, which directs the state to provide free and compulsory education to children.

questions.question: As of March 2020, the limit for Foreign Portfolio Investors' investment in corporate bonds increased to how much percentage of outstanding stock for FY 2020-21?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4. 15%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)** are institutional investors who invest in financial assets like stocks and bonds in a foreign country.
 
• As of March 2020, the Government of India increased the investment limit for FPIs in corporate bonds to **15%** of the outstanding stock for FY 2020-21.
 
• This was an increase from the earlier limit of **9%**, aimed at encouraging foreign investment in India’s corporate bond market.
 
• The decision was taken to enhance liquidity in the corporate bond market and support economic growth by providing access to additional funding sources for Indian companies.
 
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced this measure as part of its developmental and regulatory policies to strengthen the financial markets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Foreign Portfolio Investment:**

 
 
• Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) refers to investments in financial assets, such as stocks and bonds, in a foreign country by non-resident investors.
 
• FPIs are typically short-term investments and are considered more liquid compared to Foreign Direct Investment (FDI).
 
• They play a vital role in the development of domestic financial markets by providing additional capital and enhancing market depth.
 
 
 
• **Corporate Bonds in India:**
 
 
• Corporate bonds are debt securities issued by companies to raise capital for various purposes such as business expansion, working capital, or acquisitions.
 
• They are considered less risky than equity investments but carry some level of credit risk depending on the issuing company’s financial stability.
 
• In India, the corporate bond market is regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).
 
 
 
• **Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Measures:**
 
 
• The RBI often announces regulatory policies to increase foreign investments, improve liquidity, and stabilize the Indian financial markets.
 
• Increasing the FPI limit in corporate bonds was one such measure to attract foreign capital and enhance market efficiency.

questions.question: The health problem, Tinnitus, is associated with which of the following body parts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tinnitus** is a condition where a person hears ringing, buzzing, or other noises in the ears that are not caused by an external sound source.
 
• This condition is strongly associated with the **ears** and is considered an auditory issue rather than a systemic health problem.
 
• Tinnitus can occur in one or both ears and may be a symptom of underlying conditions like hearing loss, ear injury, or circulatory system disorders.
 
• It is often linked to exposure to loud noises, ageing-related hearing loss, or earwax blockage, which can affect the auditory nerves.
 
• While not typically a serious medical condition, tinnitus can significantly impact a person's quality of life, causing stress, difficulty concentrating, and sleep disturbances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Tinnitus:**

 
 
• **Subjective Tinnitus:** This is the most common type, where only the individual can hear the noise. It is often linked to problems in the outer, middle, or inner ear.
 
• **Objective Tinnitus:** A rare form of tinnitus where the doctor can hear the noise during an examination. This type is usually caused by blood vessel or muscular problems.
 
 
 
• Common Ear Diseases:
 
 
 

 **Diseases**
 **Affected area**
 
 

 Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear)
 Outer ear canal
 
 

 Otosclerosis 
 Middle ear (ossicles/tiny bones) 
 
 

 Presbycusis (Age-Related Hearing Loss) 
 Inner ear (hair cells in the cochlea)
 
 

 Otitis Media 
 Middle ear (behind the eardrum, involving the Eustachian tubes)

questions.question: The most popular festival of Kerala, Onam, is celebrated in which of the following Malayalam months?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2) Chingam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Onam** is the most prominent festival of Kerala, celebrated in the Malayalam month of **Chingam**, which typically falls in August-September.
 
• The festival marks the annual homecoming of the legendary King Mahabali, a beloved ruler in Kerala’s mythology.
 
• Onam is celebrated with great enthusiasm over ten days, with the main day, "Thiruvonam," falling on the **Chingam** month.
 
• The festival is associated with Kerala's rich cultural heritage and involves vibrant rituals, boat races, Pookalam (floral decorations), and traditional feasts called **Onasadya**.
 
• Chingam is the first month of the Malayalam calendar, and Onam’s celebration signifies the harvest season in Kerala.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **King Mahabali:**

 
 
• According to legend, Mahabali was a just and benevolent ruler whose reign was marked by equality, prosperity, and happiness in Kerala.
 
• It is believed that Lord Vishnu, in his Vamana avatar, sent Mahabali to the netherworld but granted him permission to visit his kingdom once a year, which is celebrated as Onam.
 
 
 
• **Onasadya:**
 
 
• Onasadya is a grand vegetarian feast served during Onam, consisting of multiple dishes like Avial, Sambar, Rasam, Payasam, and more, traditionally served on banana leaves.
 
• The feast is an integral part of the festival and symbolizes Kerala's culinary tradition and hospitality.
 
 
 
• **Pookalam:**
 
 
• Pookalam refers to intricate floral arrangements created in circular patterns at the entrance of homes during Onam.
 
• It symbolizes prosperity and is a tribute to King Mahabali’s homecoming.
 
 
 
• **Other Celebrations:**
 
 
• The ten-day festival includes Vallamkali (snake boat races), Pulikali (tiger dance), Kaikottikali (traditional dance), and various temple rituals.
 
• These activities highlight Kerala’s vibrant cultural and artistic heritage.

questions.question: In 1529, the Battle of Ghaghra was fought between Babur and who among the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Battle of Ghaghra (1529):** This battle was fought between Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire in India, and Muhammad Lodi, the brother of Ibrahim Lodi, who sought to regain the throne of Delhi after the defeat of Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
 
• Muhammad Lodi was supported by the Afghan chieftains and regional rulers who opposed Babur's growing dominance in the region.
 
• The battle took place near the Ghaghra River (present-day Bihar and Uttar Pradesh) and marked the final consolidation of Babur's control over northern India. *Hence, option 2 is correct.*
 
• Babur employed superior military tactics, including the effective use of gunpowder and artillery, which proved decisive in defeating the Afghan forces led by Muhammad Lodi.
 
• The victory at Ghaghra established the Mughal Empire's dominance in the region and marked the end of significant Afghan resistance to Babur's rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Babur's Military Strategy:**

 
 
• Babur introduced advanced military tactics in India, such as the use of** field artillery and the Tulughma strategy**, which involved dividing his forces into smaller units to encircle and attack the enemy.
 
• His army’s superior use of gunpowder and firearms gave him a significant advantage over traditional Indian armies that relied on cavalry and elephants.
 
 
 
• **Major battles of Babur:**
 
 
• First Battle of Panipat (**1526**): Babur's decisive victory over** Ibrahim Lodi**, the ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, is considered the beginning of Mughal rule in India. He employed gunpowder and cannons, which revolutionised Indian warfare. 
 
• Battle of Khanwa (**1527**): Babur defeated a large confederacy of Rajputs led by **Rana Sanga **of Mewar. His strategic use of artillery and muskets was key to this victory, which significantly strengthened Mughal authority in the region. 
 
• Battle of Chanderi (**1528**): Babur captured the fortress of Chanderi by defeating **Medini Rai**, a Rajput ally of Rana Sanga. This victory further cemented Mughal power and intimidated other Rajput chiefs.

questions.question: Among the following rulers, who was the author of a part of 'Kavirajamarga', the earliest known Kannada poem?

__
 
• **Amoghavarsha I**, also known as Amoghavarsha Nrupatunga, was a renowned emperor of the Rashtrakuta dynasty who ruled during the 9th century CE.
 
• He is credited with writing parts of the **'Kavirajamarga'**, the earliest known Kannada literary work, alongside his court poet Sri Vijaya.
 
• The **'Kavirajamarga'** serves as a guide to poets and scholars on Kannada poetry, grammar, and literary conventions, marking the beginning of Kannada literature.
 
• Amoghavarsha I was not only a patron of Kannada literature but also of Sanskrit. His contributions elevated the literary and cultural significance of the Rashtrakuta empire.
 
• The work highlights the regions of Karnataka where Kannada was spoken and provides insights into the socio-cultural aspects of the time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Amoghavarsha I's reign:**

 
 
• He ruled the Rashtrakuta empire from approximately 814 CE to 878 CE, achieving great prosperity and cultural advancements during his tenure.
 
• He was known for his administrative skills, religious tolerance, and promotion of art, culture, and literature.
 
 
 
• **'Kavirajamarga':**
 
 
• It is considered a landmark in Kannada literature and sets the foundation for future literary works in the Kannada language.
 
• The text is heavily influenced by Sanskrit literary traditions, showcasing the fusion of cultures under the Rashtrakuta dynasty.

__
 
• **Medium enterprises** are defined under the Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Development Act, 2006, as amended in 2020.

• Its **annual turnover** must not exceed ₹250 crore.

• The MSME sector is divided into three categories: **Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises**, based on investment and turnover thresholds.
 
• Micro enterprises: Investment up to ₹1 crore and turnover up to ₹5 crore.
 
• Small enterprises: Investment up to ₹10 crore and turnover up to ₹50 crore.
 
 
 
• **Importance of MSMEs:**
 
 
• MSMEs contribute significantly to **India's GDP**, employment generation, and exports.
 
• They are considered the **backbone of the Indian economy**, providing employment to over 11 crore people.

• Schemes like **Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE)** and the **Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP)** are aimed at supporting MSMEs.
 
 
 
• **Recent Developments:**
 
 
• The reclassification of MSMEs in 2020 introduced a **composite criteria** of investment and turnover, ensuring a broader coverage of businesses under the MSME sector.
 
• The government launched the **Aatma Nirbhar Bharat Abhiyan**, which included financial packages to boost MSMEs during the COVID-19 pandemic.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides that disputes arising out of the election of the President or Vice-President shall be decided by the Supreme Court?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 71**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 71** of the Constitution of India deals with disputes related to the election of the **President** or **Vice-President**.
 
• It states that any dispute arising out of the election of the President or Vice-President shall be decided exclusively by the **Supreme Court of India**.
 
• The decision made by the Supreme Court in such matters is **final and binding**, and no other court can have jurisdiction over such disputes.
 
• The **Supreme Court** can also declare an election void if it finds that the election process violated constitutional provisions or was marred by malpractice.
 
• This provision ensures the integrity and transparency of the electoral process for India’s highest constitutional offices. *Hence, Article 71 is directly relevant to the question.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Election of President and Vice-President:**

 
 
• The President and Vice-President of India are elected by an **electoral college** as per Articles 54 and 66, respectively, of the Constitution.
 
• The electoral college for the Presidential election consists of **elected members of Parliament** and **Legislative Assemblies of States and Union Territories** (with legislatures).
 
• For the Vice-President, the electoral college comprises **members of both Houses of Parliament**.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Supreme Court in Electoral Disputes:**
 
 
• Under Article 71, the Supreme Court exercises **exclusive jurisdiction** in resolving disputes arising out of Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections.
 
• Its role ensures that the electoral process adheres to constitutional provisions and is free from malpractices.
 
• The Supreme Court can **declare an election null and void** if it finds violations of the Constitution or election laws.
 
 
 
• **Key articles for the President:**
 
 
• Article 52: Establishes the office of the President of India.
 
• Article 53: Vests the executive power of the Union in the President.
 
• Article 54: Details the electoral college for the President's election.
 
• Article 61: Outlines the procedure for impeaching the President.
 
• Article 62: Specifies the time for holding an election to fill a vacancy in the President's office.
 
• Article 65: Allows the Vice-President to act as President or discharge presidential functions.
 
• Article 71: Deals with matters relating to the election of the President and Vice-President.
 
• Article 72: Grants the President the power to pardon, suspend, remit, or commute sentences.
 
• Article 123: Gives the President the power to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session. 
 
 
 
• **Key articles for the Vice-President:**
 
 
• Article 63: States that there shall be a Vice-President of India.
 
• Article 64: Makes the Vice-President the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).
 
• Article 65: Allows the Vice-President to act as President in case of the President's absence or illness.
 
• Article 66: Governs the election of the Vice-President.
 
• Article 67: Specifies the term of office for the Vice-President.

questions.question: In which year was the Treaty of Purandar signed between Rajput ruler and commander of Mughal Empire Jai Singh I and Maratha Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Treaty of Purandar** was signed in **1665** between the Maratha ruler Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and the Mughal Empire's commander, Jai Singh I.
 
• This treaty marked the agreement where Shivaji ceded 23 forts and the surrounding territories to the Mughal Empire, retaining only 12 forts.
 
• Shivaji also agreed to serve as a vassal of the Mughals and assist them in their campaigns in the Deccan region.
 
• The treaty was signed after Jai Singh I, a trusted general of Aurangzeb, launched a military campaign against Shivaji, forcing him to negotiate.
 
• The Treaty of Purandar is considered a turning point in Shivaji's career, as it temporarily brought the Marathas under the influence of the Mughals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key treaties and alliances between the Mughals and Rajputs:** 

 
 
• **Mughal-Mewar Peace Treaty (1615)**

 
 
• Between: Mughal Emperor Jahangir and Maharana Amar Singh I of Mewar.
 
• Outcome: Ended the long-standing war between Mewar and the Mughals. Mewar was returned to the Maharana, but his son, Karan Singh, was sent to the Mughal court, and the fort of Chittor was not to be repaired.
 
 
 
• **Mughal-Amber Alliance (1562)**
 
 
• Between: Mughal Emperor Akbar and Raja Bharmal of Amber.
 
• Outcome: Marked the first formal acceptance of Mughal suzerainty by a Rajput state, solidifying ties through a matrimonial alliance with Raja Bharmal's daughter, Harkha Bai (Jodha Bai).
 
 
 
• **Treaty of Purandar (1665)**
 
 
• Between: The Mughal commander Mirza Raja Jai Singh I and the Maratha leader Shivaji.
 
• Outcome: Shivaji was forced to sign the agreement after Jai Singh besieged the fort of Purandar.

questions.question: Which of the following is the instrument used to measure temperature variations due to sky conditions?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Aethrioscope** is an instrument used to measure temperature variations caused by changes in sky conditions, particularly cloud cover.
 
• It was invented by Sir John Leslie, a Scottish physicist, in the 19th century to study meteorological phenomena.
 
• The Aethrioscope works by measuring the cooling effect of radiation emitted from the sky, which varies depending on whether the sky is clear or cloudy.
 
• It is particularly useful in determining nocturnal cooling, as cloud cover can significantly reduce heat loss from the Earth during nighttime.
 
• This device is not commonly used in modern meteorology but is historically significant for understanding atmospheric conditions and radiation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Actinometer:**

 
 
• An actinometer is used to measure the intensity of solar radiation, not temperature variations.
 
• It is commonly used in meteorology and climatology to study solar energy and radiation levels.
 
 
 
• **Acetimeter:**
 
 
• This instrument is used to measure the concentration of acetic acid in solutions, particularly in the vinegar industry.
 
• It has no relation to meteorological phenomena or temperature variations.
 
 
 
• **Algometer:**
 
 
• An algometer measures pain sensitivity or pain threshold in humans, primarily in medical studies.

__
 
• **The Badami Cave Temples** were built during the reign of the early Chalukya dynasty in the 6th century CE.
 
• **Mangalesha,** the younger brother of Pulakeshin I, is credited with constructing the cave temples at Badami.
 
• The temples are a blend of **Dravidian and Nagara architectural styles,** showcasing the cultural and religious advancements of the Chalukyas.
 
• Mangalesha, a ruler known for his patronage of art and religion, built these temples primarily to honor **Hindu deities and Jain Tirthankaras.**
 
• The Badami Cave Temples are a group of four temples, of which three are dedicated to **Hindu gods (Shiva and Vishnu)**, and one is dedicated to Jainism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chalukya Dynasty:**

 
 
• The early Chalukyas ruled large parts of South and Central India between the 6th and 8th centuries CE, with Badami (formerly Vatapi) as their capital.
 
 
 
• **Four Caves at Badami:**
 
 
• Cave 1: Dedicated to Lord Shiva, featuring carvings of Shiva in various forms, including Nataraja.
 
• Cave 2: Dedicated to Lord Vishnu, showing his incarnations such as Trivikrama and Varaha.
 
• Cave 3: The largest and most elaborate, featuring intricate carvings of Vishnu in different forms, including Narasimha and Trivikrama.
 
• Cave 4: Dedicated to Jain Tirthankaras, including a carving of Mahavira.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO Heritage Status:**
 
 
• The Badami Cave Temples are considered one of the finest examples of rock-cut architecture in India and are a contender for inclusion in the UNESCO World Heritage Sites list.
 
 
 
• **Vikramaditya:**
 
 
• ​Vikramaditya II brought sculptors from the defeated Kanchipuram to his capital, where they helped perfect the **Dravidian-style architecture** seen in the **Virupaksha temple**, which in turn inspired the later **Kailasanatha temple at Ellora.** 
 
 
 
• **Pulakeshin:**
 
 
• His reign saw the construction of numerous temples in the **Chalukyan style at Aihole** and the excavation of the Badami cave temples, which are noted for their intricate carvings and depictions of Hindu gods, and include a mix of Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain shrines​.
 
 
 
• Kirtivarman:
 
 
• Kirtivarman I initiated the construction of the cave temples at Badami and was a major patron of the developing Chalukyan architectural style, which laid the foundation for the region's unique blend of **Nagara and Dravida** traditions. ​
